passage:
At nine, Gautam brought home a science paper with one wrong answer circled in red. His parents, Pradeep and Sangeeta, studied it and asked, "Why did you lose that mark?" Neither asked what he liked about the experiment. After that, Gautam folded such papers small and hid them in his atlas, and learned to say, "Nothing much."

At twenty-one, Gautam was given a project on water use in his city. He researched for three weeks, redrew the outline eleven times and told his roommate, "It's not ready to show anyone yet." Every version looked flawed to him: the second heading was clumsy, the third source felt weak. Other students were already drafting. Reading one more article seemed safer than writing a single paragraph that could be marked down.

On the deadline's eve Gautam looked at the tidy, untouched document and thought of the atlas. He opened a blank page and typed a rough sentence anyway, though his stomach was tight.

qa.q: How many times did Gautam redraw the outline?
qa.a: He redrew the outline eleven times.

qa.q: How is the way Gautam hid papers at nine linked to his endless preparation at twenty-one?
qa.a: At nine Gautam learns that love and approval follow marks, so he hides mistakes; at twenty-one the same fear of a marked-down page keeps him researching and redrawing the outline rather than starting, which is perfectionism as paralysis.

qa.q: What was Gautam probably feeling as he told his roommate the outline was not ready to show anyone?
qa.a: Gautam was afraid of being judged, so preparing felt safer than exposing a rough draft.

qa.q: What small step did Gautam take on the eve of the deadline, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He opened a blank page and typed a rough sentence, which breaks the cycle of preparing because a rough start is easier than a perfect one.

grounding: Perfectionism linked across ages: a child whose parents respond only to marks learns to hide mistakes, and the young adult later postpones starting through endless preparation.
